# Redesign the SaveIt.now landing page

You are working in a self-contained Vite, React, and TypeScript application. It contains the former SaveIt.now landing page, whose hero uses a dark orange gradient, plus six original campaign images in `public/images/landing-v2/`.

Redesign only this landing page into a complete, premium, modern, new-generation product site. Audit every supplied image before deciding how to use it, then use the set purposefully throughout the experience rather than treating the images as a generic gallery. The visual language should feel cinematic, energetic, editorial, and highly crafted, with the kind of confident art direction associated with a major contemporary consumer brand campaign. Keep SaveIt.now recognizable and make the page feel cohesive from hero through footer.

SaveIt.now is "your home for bookmarks." Its differentiated promise has two connected sides:

1. Agentic bookmarking: a user only saves something. The product handles capture, understanding, categorization, organization, and retrieval without manual filing.
2. A polished iOS experience: saving and rediscovering should feel immediate and native wherever the user is.

The central idea is simple: no manual work, just "Save it." The page should make visitors believe they can retrieve what they saved instead of losing it in folders, tabs, or forgotten bookmark lists. Express the strong "100% promise" as an aspirational product promise about rediscovery and confidence, without inventing unsupported statistics, testimonials, guarantees, or urgency.

Use conversion-focused copywriting. Lead with one clear promise, sell the lived transformation before listing features, and keep the reading rhythm concise. Do not use em dashes anywhere in the copy. Avoid vague phrases that do not explain the product. All visible product copy must be in English.

The finished page must include:

- a distinctive hero with a strong headline, concise support copy, primary CTA, secondary CTA, and a premium campaign-style use of the supplied imagery
- a clear explanation of the agentic workflow and the "just save it" mechanism
- a visually memorable section for the 100% rediscovery promise
- an iOS section that presents the mobile side credibly without fabricating a fake screenshot of the actual app
- pricing with a free tier and a $5 per month Pro tier billed annually
- an elegant, interactive FAQ treatment
- a polished closing CTA and footer

Preserve or improve useful interactions. Add purposeful motion and responsive behavior, with reduced-motion support. Make navigation and calls to action functional. Ensure the design works at desktop and mobile widths, remains accessible, and has no obvious overflow or unreadable contrast. Keep the implementation maintainable and use the existing stack.

Work only inside the current working directory. Do not edit files outside the current working directory.
During setup, configure your app and package scripts to use port 9322, then use that port for runtime verification.
Use pnpm exclusively if dependency installation or package scripts are needed. Do not use npm.
Set the browser title and the primary visible title to your model name, using only identity information already available to you. Add nothing else to either title.
Run the relevant checks yourself. Do not edit files outside the current working directory.

# Baseline provenance

This Vite app isolates the SaveIt.now landing page as it existed at Git commit
`88ee367`, immediately before the landing redesign commit `2c15af4`.

The baseline intentionally retains the dark page and orange-gradient hero. The
six images under `public/images/landing-v2/` came from the original
`landing_v2/` art folder and are supplied as raw redesign material.

Image inventory:

- `observatory.png`: hilltop observatory with a glowing arc
- `lake.png`: coral-lit mountain lake
- `home.png`: small illuminated house on a flowered hill
- `portal-arch.png`: glowing arch among rocks and flowers
- `portal-ridge.png`: glowing rectangular portal on a ridge
- `portal-rocks.png`: pale portal framed by rocks and vegetation

text: These
images are gorgeous but huge—3272x1834 at 5-10MB each, way too big to ship raw. I need to generate optimized WebP versions alongside the originals in

public/images/landing-v2/, keeping originals untouched while creating ~1920px width derivatives using cwebp. I'm going through each image to audit its content and mood, starting with portal-ridge.png,
a glowing orange-pink portal on a ridge that feels like the strongest hero image.
Now I'm m
apping the
r
est:
portal-arch fits the rediscovery/closing CTA, portal-rocks suits the entry or iOS section, home.png works for the closing "home for bookmarks" section,

lake.png suits calm/pricing backdrops, and observatory.png fits the agentic understanding section. My plan is to build the hero around portal-ridge with gradient overlays and a headline, making sure the browser title reflects the model name.
Since
the inst
ructions require the h1 to actually be the model name "Claude Fable 5.1", I'll set that as the primary display title and place the marketing tagline as a secondary display
line beneath it, keeping the design impact while following the naming requirement. For the "just save it" agentic workflow section, I'm pairing it with the observatory image since
it evokes the agent seeing and understanding.
For
the four

-step flow of Save, Understand, Organize, Retrieve, I want an interactive demo showing a URL being saved and auto-tagged, possibly with clickable tabs revealing detail alongside the image. For the "100% back
when you need it" promise, I'm pairing it with the portal-arch image and a big typographic "100%" statement, plus a search-style interactive demo with rotating example queries and result chips to
make the aspiration tangible. For the iOS section, I'm considering the portal-rocks or lake image and thinking about how to represent a share-sheet flow credibly using
a stylized device frame rather than a fake screenshot, making clear it's schematic.
I
'm being

careful not to invent features—sticking to safe, plausible claims like saving from the share sheet, searching everything saved, and syncing with the web extension, since the site does link to an iOS app. I
may skip device frames entirely and use simple feature cards instead to avoid overstating what the app does.
For
pricing, I'll ke
ep it to
Free / Pro at
$5/mo billed ann
ually ($60/yr)
ex
actly as specified, avoiding the temptation to invent a monthly price toggle that wasn't given.
For the FAQ,
I'll build

an accordion with animated height transitions, proper aria-expanded attributes, and keyboard accessibility, then close with a CTA and footer.

I'm also planning the header as s
ticky with anchor navigation to each section, a mobile menu toggle, and a CTA linking to signin with a signup intent. For motion, I'll use an IntersectionObserver reve
al hook, scroll-based parallax on the hero that respects reduced-motion preferences, and CSS-driven glow animations. For images, I'm considering generating optimized webp der
ivatives at multiple widths for responsive srcset usage while keeping the originals intact.
I'
m deciding to skip bl
urred placeholder images and instead use simple CSS background color placeholders. I need to set the dev server and preview to run
on port 9322 in the vite config and scripts. For fonts, I'm weighing whether to add an editorial serif alongside Geist for a display accent -
- looking at Instrument Serif as a non-variable font option and considering installing that package to get an italic serif accent for the editorial feel.
Now
I'm planning cleanup and file structure: I'll delete unused components like landing-stats, why-saveit, extensions-section, and how-it-works using the safe delete tool rather than
rm, then lay out the new source files -- App.tsx, a styles file with tokens and keyframes and reveal utilities, hooks for intersection-based reveal and reduced motion, and an image manif
est module.
I
'm s
ketching out the component breakdown: header, hero, an agentic workflow section, a promise section, iOS section, pricing, FAQ, closing CTA, footer, a responsive image
component, and the existing app button. I'm settling on a near-black plum base with ember orange, blush, and cream accents for the palette.
Now
I
'm drafting the hero copy without em dashes, testing eyebrow text and a headline around "Claude Fable 5.1", then working through ta
glines like "Just save it. It comes back when you need it." for the supporting message, plus a subhead about capturing and organizing sa
ves without folders or tags.
For
the CTA
s, I'm settling on "Start saving free" linking to signup and "See how it works" jumping to a workflow anchor, with a trust line about the free plan needing no credit card.

Then I move into the workflow section, drafting an eyebrow and heading "You do one thing. Save it." and sketching the interactive step cards — starting with "Save" and "Understand" descriptions before contin
uing to the next step.
I
fin
ish the four workflow steps (Organize, Retrieve) with copy about auto-filled metadata and plain-language search, plus a live capture dem
o card. Then I move into the "100%" promise section, trying out different phrasings for the eyebrow and headline while worrying that
a literal "100%" guarantee sounds too absolute.
I
settle on "100%" as a huge display number followed by "of what you save should be findable. That is the standard we build for," paired with three supporting pillars around semantic search, pl
ain-language questions, and no folders — plus an interactive demo with clickable example questions that reveal text-only result cards, avoiding external image dependencies. For
the iOS section, I decide to reuse the portal-rocks image for its bright, portable feel.
For the six
images across sections, I map each to its purpose: ridge for hero, observatory for workflow, arch for the promise section, rocks for iOS (the path suggesting the share-sheet flow), a d
immed lake panel for calm pricing, and home for the closing CTA. Then I draft the iOS copy — a headline about saving from anywhere on iPhone, supporting text about sharing from Safari,
YouTube, or X and having everything ready later, plus a feature list covering share sheet saving, plain-language search, and shared library across web and extension.
For p
ricing, I'm
laying out Free vs Pro tiers pulling numbers straight from the original copy — bookmarks, AI runs, chat questions, extension/app access for
Free, and higher limits plus API access, CSV export, and priority support for Pro at $5/month billed annually. For the FAQ, I plan to adapt the original answers while cleaning up stray
em dashes and hyphens for consistency.
Mo
ving to the closing CTA, footer, and header sections, I'm keeping the "home for bookmarks" messaging, fixing the "Comparaison" typo to "Comparison" in the
footer, and confirming the header nav items (How it works, Promise, iOS, Pricing, FAQ, Sign in, Start free) along with a mobile hamburger menu. Now I'm put
ting together shell commands to batch-convert the landing page images into resized webp versions at different quality levels.
I've
m

apped all six sunset-palette renders to their sections (portal-ridge to hero, observatory to agentic workflow, portal-arch to the rediscovery promise, portal-rocks to iOS, lake to pricing, home to the
closing CTA). Since the PNGs are 5-10MB each, I'll generate WebP derivatives alongside them and then set up ports, fonts, and images.

---
name: dev-browser
description: "Browser automation with persistent page state using dev-browser CLI. Use when user mentions 'browse', 'open website', 'click on', 'fill form', 'take screenshot', 'scrape', 'automate browser', 'test website', 'log into', 'navigate to', 'web page', 'dev-browser', or any browser interaction task."
allowed-tools:
  - Bash(dev-browser *)
  - Bash(/Applications/Helium.app/Contents/MacOS/Helium *)
---

# dev-browser

Browser automation tool that controls browsers through sandboxed JavaScript scripts via CLI.
Scripts run in QuickJS WASM sandbox - not Node.js. No `require`, `fetch`, `fs`, or `process`.

## Setup

If `dev-browser` is not found:

- First check the repository's package-manager rules. If the repo forbids npm
  or requires pnpm-only commands, do not run `npm install -g`.
- In Codex, prefer the bundled workspace runtime when available: use the local
  Node/Playwright/Chromium dependencies to perform the same page-load,
  screenshot, console-error, and interaction checks without installing
  anything.
- Only install the CLI when npm is allowed for the current workspace and the
  task really needs `dev-browser` persistence or CDP attachment that the
  bundled browser runtime cannot provide.

```bash
npm install -g dev-browser
dev-browser install
```

When falling back to Playwright, preserve the same proof standard: record the
URL, title, console/page errors, screenshots or output artifacts, and the exact
interaction steps that were executed. State clearly that the `dev-browser` CLI
was unavailable and that the fallback used real browser automation.

## Core Pattern

Write small, focused scripts. Each script does ONE thing. End by logging state for next decision.

```bash
dev-browser <<'EOF'
const page = await browser.getPage("main");
await page.goto("https://example.com");
console.log(JSON.stringify({ url: page.url(), title: await page.title() }, null, 2));
EOF
```

## CLI Flags

| Flag | Description |
|------|-------------|
| `--headless` | Launch Chromium in headless mode |
| `--connect [URL]` | Connect to running Chrome/Chromium via CDP (auto-discover Chrome, or use a specific CDP endpoint) |
| `--browser <NAME>` | Select named browser instance (default: "default") |
| `--timeout <SECONDS>` | Max script execution time (default: 30) |

## Browser API

| Method | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| `browser.getPage(name)` | Get/create named page (persists between scripts) |
| `browser.newPage()` | Create anonymous page (auto-cleanup after script) |
| `browser.listPages()` | List all tabs: `[{id, url, title, name}]` |
| `browser.closePage(name)` | Close named page |

## File I/O (restricted to `~/.dev-browser/tmp/`)

Never pass absolute paths to `saveScreenshot` or `writeFile`. If a task asks for screenshots or reports in a scratchpad/output directory, save with a relative name first, then copy the returned `~/.dev-browser/tmp/...` file to the requested path from the shell.

| Method | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| `await saveScreenshot(buf, name)` | Save screenshot buffer, returns path |
| `await writeFile(name, data)` | Write file, returns path |
| `await readFile(name)` | Read file, returns content |

## Key Workflows

### Discover Unknown Page

```bash
dev-browser <<'EOF'
const page = await browser.getPage("main");
await page.goto("https://example.com");
const result = await page.snapshotForAI();
console.log(result.full);
EOF
```

Then interact based on discovered elements:
```bash
dev-browser <<'EOF'
const page = await browser.getPage("main");
await page.getByRole("button", { name: "Continue" }).click();
const result = await page.snapshotForAI({ track: "main" });
console.log(result.full);
EOF
```

### Take Screenshot

```bash
dev-browser <<'EOF'
const page = await browser.getPage("main");
const buf = await page.screenshot();
const path = await saveScreenshot(buf, "debug.png");
console.log(path);
EOF
```

### Fill Form

```bash
dev-browser <<'EOF'
const page = await browser.getPage("main");
await page.fill("#email", "user@example.com");
await page.fill("#password", "secret");
await page.click("button[type=submit]");
await page.waitForURL("**/dashboard");
console.log(JSON.stringify({ url: page.url(), title: await page.title() }, null, 2));
EOF
```

### Connect to Running Chrome

```bash
dev-browser --connect <<'EOF'
const tabs = await browser.listPages();
console.log(JSON.stringify(tabs, null, 2));
EOF
```

### Connect to Helium via CDP

Helium is Chromium-based and can be controlled by `dev-browser` when launched with remote debugging enabled. `dev-browser --connect` auto-discovery does not find Helium, so always pass the explicit CDP endpoint.

For a separate automation profile:
```bash
"/Applications/Helium.app/Contents/MacOS/Helium" \
  --remote-debugging-port=9334 \
  --user-data-dir=/tmp/helium-dev-browser-profile \
  --no-first-run \
  --no-default-browser-check
```

Then connect:
```bash
dev-browser --browser helium --connect http://127.0.0.1:9334 <<'EOF'
const tabs = await browser.listPages();
console.log(JSON.stringify(tabs, null, 2));
EOF
```

To automate the user's existing Helium session, Helium must be fully quit and relaunched with `--remote-debugging-port`; an already-running Helium instance that was started without remote debugging cannot be attached by `dev-browser`.

```bash
"/Applications/Helium.app/Contents/MacOS/Helium" --remote-debugging-port=9334
dev-browser --browser helium --connect http://127.0.0.1:9334
```

If Helium is already open without CDP and must not be restarted, use AppleScript or Computer Use for UI-level control instead of `dev-browser`.

### Error Recovery

If a script fails, the page stays where it stopped. Reconnect and inspect:
```bash
dev-browser <<'EOF'
const page = await browser.getPage("main");
const path = await saveScreenshot(await page.screenshot(), "debug.png");
console.log(JSON.stringify({ screenshot: path, url: page.url(), title: await page.title() }, null, 2));
EOF
```

## Tips

- Use `page.snapshotForAI()` for structure discovery; use screenshots for visual layout
- Keep page names stable across scripts to resume after failures
- Use `console.log(JSON.stringify(...))` for structured output
- Use `--timeout 10` for scripts that should fail fast
- Pages from `browser.getPage("name")` persist between script runs - no need to re-navigate
- Inside `page.evaluate(...)`, use plain JavaScript only - no TypeScript

## Full API Reference

For complete Playwright Page methods and advanced patterns, see [references/api-reference.md](references/api-reference.md).

## What shipped

**Image audit and placement** (all six used, each with a job):
- `portal-ridge` (ember door on a ridge): hero, parallax full-bleed, keeps the legacy orange identity
- `observatory` (arc that sees everything): agentic workflow stage
- `portal-arch`: backdrop for the 100% promise
- `portal-rocks` (path into a bright door): iOS section
- `lake` (calm, reflective): pricing panel
- `home` (lit house): closing CTA, "your home for bookmarks"

Originals untouched; the page renders `cwebp` derivatives in `public/images/landing-v2/web/` (1920w, 1080w, blur placeholder) so the 47 MB of PNGs never hit the wire.

**Sections** (`src/components/`):
- `landing-header`: floating pill nav, scroll-aware blur, mobile menu with Escape/resize close and body scroll lock
- `landing-hero`: h1 and `<title>` are `Claude Fable 5.1`; promise line, support copy, two CTAs, "save anything" ticker
- `workflow-section`: 4-step auto-advancing stepper (click pins it) driving a live capture card that fills in title, summary, tags, then answers a plain-language query
- `promise-section`: giant "100%" typographic, typed query demo with clickable example chips, three pillars
- `ios-section`: schematic phone with abstract share sheet, explicitly labeled "not a screenshot"
- `landing-pricing`: Free and Pro at $5/month billed annually ($60), limits taken from the original copy
- `faq`: accessible accordion (`aria-expanded`/`aria-controls`, grid-rows height animation)
- `closing-cta`, `footer`

**Motion and a11y**: IntersectionObserver reveals, hero parallax via rAF, CSS keyframes, all gated by `prefers-reduced-motion` (verified: no marquee, no auto-advance, everything visible). Skip link, focus rings, one h1, all images have alt, in-page anchors resolve.

**Verification**: `tsc -b && vite build` passes; dev and preview both on `127.0.0.1:9322` (HTTP 200, zero console errors); screenshots at 1440 and 390 with no horizontal overflow; interactions tested (menu nav, step pinning, FAQ toggle, query chips). No em dashes in copy.

One thing worth flagging: I found and fixed a Tailwind class-ordering bug in my own `CampaignPicture` (base `relative` was beating callers' `absolute`), and the "Sign in" hide-on-mobile had the same class of issue. Both are now structural rather than relying on class precedence.Those two notifications are just the dev and preview servers I stopped myself after verification (they exit with a non-zero code when killed). Nothing is running on 9322 now, and no follow-up is needed.

Summary stands: the redesigned SaveIt.now landing page builds cleanly, serves on `127.0.0.1:9322` in both dev and preview, passes desktop/mobile/reduced-motion checks, and all changes are confined to this directory.
